Real and Unreal Conditionals

You can use the Real conditional with If clauses to talk situations and outcomes.
The Real Conditional can be used to connect actions and consequences together.
You can talk about possible future event with a Present Perfect verb in the If clause and a future form in the main clause.
You use the Unreal Conditional to express imaginary or future situations.
You use the Unreal Conditional to talk about events that are impossible situations in the present or events unlikely to happen in the future.
If you could write a successful script about a manned mission to the red planet and have it filmed on a stage with green screen technology, wouldn't you jump at the chance?
You use the Real Conditional to say it's possible that you will or will not do something. In that condition, something else may, may not will or will not happen.

The parts of the sentence are divided into two clauses: the If clause and the Condition clause.
Structure:
If + Present Simple/Present continuous … will/Present Continuous / be going to
Example:
We'll need a holographic TV if we're going to keep up.

You can use an Imperative verb in the main clause if you are making offers, giving instructions, or suggesting advice.
Example:
Get one of these if you want to save water.

You can use a verb in the Present Perfect with the if- clause to suggest that the action needs to be completed before the situation in the main clause can be true.
Structure: If+ Present/Present Perfect … Future form (will, Present Continuous, be going to)

The Unreal Conditional is also called the second conditional.
Structure:
If… Simple Past, … would+verb or Would+verb … if … Simple Past.
Example:
If scientists knew for sure they wouldn't have to keep looking for answers.

You use If … were + to + infinitive to talk about imaginary future situations, especially when it is not likely the situation will happen.
Example:
If you were to stand in a crowded area and watch the people, what would you see?

You use if it was not for + noun phrase to say that one situation depends on another situation or person to come true. You use If it weren't for … if you want to express yourself more formally.
Example:
If it weren't for overzealous reporters making fun of stories, more people wouldn't be worrying about telling them.
If I knew I could write earlier, this wouldn't be my first day on a movie set.
Verbs Followed by -ing and To-Infinitives
When you talk about two actions linked together, you normally use two verbs. The first verb follows the rules of conjugation for the sentence, while the second verb can be a verb in the -ing form.
Other writers and directors keep putting out bigger and bigger films.
You can use two verbs to talk about two connected actions. The main verb introduces the main action, and the second verb in the -ing form gives more information about that action.

You can use a variety of verbs followed by a verb in the -ing form. Some of these verbs are related in meaning, or have opposite meanings, like: like/dislike, start/stop, can't bear/stand, love/adore/hate, allow/forbid, admit/deny, quit/finish, appreciate/resent ...

You can often put an object between the two verbs. You can use pronouns and possessives.
Structure: Subject + first verb + object + -ing form of the second verb
Example: Have you ever observed someone gazing into the night sky with longing?
Prepositional verbs are always followed by another verb in the -ing form like end up, carry on, keep on, go on, succeed in, depend on, adjust to, put off …
Some verbs can be followed by either an -ing verb or to+Infinitive, like like, love, hate, dislike, intend, dread, advise, recommend, regret … The difference in meaning depends on the preceding verb.
Forget/Remember with to+Infinitive are looking forward into a future situation. With an -ing form they refer to a past action.
Advise/Recommend with to+Infinitive are followed by an object. With an -ing form there is no object.
Regret with to+Infinitive is a polite form of apology. With an -ing form it has the meaning of If only this hadn't happened.

images.text: Had it not been for sci-fi books and movies, I would have never learned to read or become interested in films. If I knew then what I know now about the sci-fi industry, I would have decided on going into filmmaking long ago. Should you see me at the movies gazing lovingly at the screen, understand that it is because I almost missed my calling! Supposing you were desperate to work on a sci-fi film and had never had the chance, what would you do? If you could write a successful script about a manned mission to the red planet and have it filmed on a stage with green screen technology, wouldn't you jump at the chance? If I had started writing earlier, this may not have been my first day on a movie set.

Supposing you were to make a movie with special effects. What would you hope to show? What would you expect to achieve? How much of the budget would you be forced to spend on them? Other writers and directors keep putting out bigger and bigger films. It's hard to imagine topping one of the biggies, but you have to try. I have actually succeeded in coming up with an exciting sci-fi story and now I am depending on having the special effects artists bring it to life.

If you had proposed my doing this even five years ago I would have thought you were crazy. If you looked back at me in those days, you would have seen one unhappy guy. If you've taken a look at me today, you see I'm not complaining about working long hours any more. Were it not for a bit of luck I would still be regretting not taking a chance. Today we're editing a scene with meteorites that materialize in the blink of an eye. Tomorrow we're taking on the extraterrestrials! If you have an idea for a sci-fi blockbuster film, take a chance. I did, now look where I am!
